scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Rates, One Crossing' over a cartoon of a large green island near a mainland and a small island far out at sea. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: BLUE line = immigration of new species, I(S); RED line = local extinction, E(S); GOLD dot = the crossing, S* ('S star'); horizontal axis 'species on the island, S' from 0 to P; vertical axis 'species per day'. Mainland at left, island centre-right, sea pale teal between. Species are small coloured round tokens. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Curves are computed from I(S) = 10(1 - S/100) and E(S) = 0.1S with P = 100 and labelled 'computed, illustrative numbers'; islands, animals and tokens are cartoons labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Why does a big island near a mainland hold more kinds of animals than a small, remote one? One process can give both patterns. It is a balance between two rates.
scenes.visual: Two islands side by side: a large one close to the mainland covered in many differently coloured tokens, and a small one far out with only a few. Counters above them tick up to show many versus few kinds (schematic). A question mark floats between them, then splits into a BLUE arrow and a RED arrow.
scenes.narration: Why does a big island near a mainland hold more kinds of animals than a small, remote one? One process can give both patterns. It is a balance between two rates.

scenes.tts: Start with the mainland. It holds a pool of species that could reach the island, P species in all. The number living on the island is S, its species richness.
scenes.visual: The mainland at left fills with 100 tokens in many colours; label 'species pool, P = 100'. An empty island at centre-right; a counter on it reads 'S = 0'. Labels 'P: species that could arrive' and 'S: species living on the island' appear in turn.
scenes.narration: Start with the mainland. It holds a pool of species that could reach the island, P species in all. The number living on the island is S, its species richness.

scenes.tts: Now let animals cross the water. On an empty island, every arrival belongs to a new species, so the count climbs fast. Immigration, here, means only the arrival of a species not already present.
scenes.visual: Tokens fly one at a time from mainland to island along dotted arcs. Each one that lands on the empty island lights up and the counter S ticks up quickly: 1, 2, 3, 4. Caption on screen: 'immigration = arrival of a NEW species'.
scenes.narration: Now let animals cross the water. On an empty island, every arrival belongs to a new species, so the count climbs fast. Immigration, here, means only the arrival of a species not already present.

scenes.tts: As the island fills, more arrivals belong to species already there. An arrival of a kind already present changes nothing in the count. So new arrivals slow, and stop when all P species live there.
scenes.visual: The island now holds many tokens. Most incoming tokens match a colour already present and land without moving the species counter, labelled 'species already here: no new species'; only an occasional new colour lights up. The counter climbs more slowly. A final frame shows every pool colour on the island and no token lighting up: 'S = P: no new species left'.
scenes.narration: As the island fills, more arrivals belong to species already there. An arrival of a kind already present changes nothing in the count. So new arrivals slow, and stop when all P species live there.

scenes.tts: Plot that rate of new arrivals against the number of species on the island. The blue line starts high on an empty island and falls to zero when S reaches P.
scenes.visual: The axes slide in below the island. A BLUE dot traces the immigration rate point by point as the counter rises, drawing a straight BLUE line from 10 at S = 0 down to 0 at S = 100 (computed). Label 'I(S): new species arriving per day'.
scenes.narration: Plot that rate of new arrivals against the number of species on the island. The blue line starts high on an empty island and falls to zero when S reaches P.

scenes.tts: Residents also disappear. This is local extinction, a loss from this island only. Suppose each resident has the same, independent chance of being lost. Then more residents mean more losses, and the red line rises.
scenes.visual: Tokens on the island blink out one at a time, labelled 'lost from this island only'; on the mainland the same colours stay lit. With few tokens the blinks are rare; with many they come quickly. A RED line rises from 0 at S = 0 to 10 at S = 100 (computed). Label 'E(S): residents lost per day'.
scenes.narration: Residents also disappear. This is local extinction, a loss from this island only. Suppose each resident has the same, independent chance of being lost. Then more residents mean more losses, and the red line rises.

scenes.tts: Where the blue line meets the red, new arrivals equal losses. That richness is the equilibrium, S star. Below it, arrivals win and the count climbs. Above it, losses win and the count falls back.
scenes.visual: A GOLD dot appears where BLUE and RED cross, at S = 50, with a dashed drop line to the axis labelled 'S*'. Arrows on the S axis point toward S* from both sides: left of S* 'arrivals > losses: S rises'; right of S* 'losses > arrivals: S falls'.
scenes.narration: Where the blue line meets the red, new arrivals equal losses. That richness is the equilibrium, S star. Below it, arrivals win and the count climbs. Above it, losses win and the count falls back.

scenes.tts: At the crossing, nothing stops. Species keep arriving and keep vanishing, at the same rate. That shared rate is the turnover. The count settles near S star and wobbles a little, while the list keeps changing.
scenes.visual: The island at S*: tokens still fly in and others blink out at an equal pace. The counter hovers near 50, flickering between about 46 and 54 (labelled 'chance version, schematic'). Beside the island a small list of colour swatches keeps changing while its length stays near 50. Label 'turnover = I(S*) = E(S*)'.
scenes.narration: At the crossing, nothing stops. Species keep arriving and keep vanishing, at the same rate. That shared rate is the turnover. The count settles near S star and wobbles a little, while the list keeps changing.

scenes.tts: Now push the island farther from the mainland, keeping its size the same. Which line moves, and which way does the gold point go?
scenes.visual: The island slides slowly to the right, away from the mainland; the dotted flight arcs stretch and thin. The graph shows the original BLUE and RED lines and the GOLD dot with a large question mark beside the dot.
scenes.narration: Now push the island farther from the mainland, keeping its size the same. Which line moves, and which way does the gold point go?

scenes.visual: Hold on the far-away island and the graph with the question mark; a small 5-second timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: Fewer new species reach a distant island at every richness. So the blue line drops, the crossing slides left, and S star falls. The far island holds fewer species.
scenes.visual: The BLUE line pivots down to a lower line (from 5 at S = 0 to 0 at S = 100, computed). The GOLD dot slides left along the RED line to S = 33. On-screen: 'farther: S* 50 to 33'. The original BLUE line remains faint for comparison.
scenes.narration: Fewer new species reach a distant island at every richness. So the blue line drops, the crossing slides left, and S star falls. The far island holds fewer species.

scenes.tts: Now keep the distance and shrink the island instead. A small island loses residents faster at every richness. The red line rises, and S star moves left again.
scenes.visual: Reset to the original BLUE line. The island shrinks in place. The RED line steepens (to 20 at S = 100, computed) and the GOLD dot slides left to S = 33. On-screen: 'smaller: S* 50 to 33'. The original RED line stays faint.
scenes.narration: Now keep the distance and shrink the island instead. A small island loses residents faster at every richness. The red line rises, and S star moves left again.

scenes.tts: So near, large islands hold the most species, and far, small ones the fewest. One balance of two rates gives both of the old patterns.
scenes.visual: Split screen: a near, large island with its graph (high BLUE, low RED, GOLD dot far right, label 'high S*') beside a far, small island with its graph (low BLUE, steep RED, GOLD dot far left, label 'low S*'). Token counts on the islands match: many versus few.
scenes.narration: So near, large islands hold the most species, and far, small ones the fewest. One balance of two rates gives both of the old patterns.

scenes.tts: Keep the scope. This is a model. It leaves out new species forming on the island. Real curves need not be straight, because species differ and affect one another. And it predicts how many species, not which ones.
scenes.visual: A small caption appears first: 'not included: new species forming on the island'. The straight BLUE and RED lines bend into gentle curves labelled 'real curves: not necessarily straight (schematic)'. Then the island's token list appears with a big count '50' beside it, and the colour swatches carry a label 'which species: not predicted'.
scenes.narration: Keep the scope. This is a model. It leaves out new species forming on the island. Real curves need not be straight, because species differ and affect one another. And it predicts how many species, not which ones.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Species count settles where new arrivals equal local losses.'
